name: Starter: Italian
about: Italian in real, everyday sentences, with each one's words in Italian order.

words.stare: to stay; to be (how someone is); with -ando or -endo: to be doing
words.piacere: pleasure; to please; mi piace: I like
words.conoscere: to know (a person, a place); to meet
words.vedersi: to see each other; to meet
words.mare: sea; al mare: to the beach

piacere-di-conoscerti.about: Literally pleasure of knowing you; Piacere! alone works too.

per-favore.about: Literally for favor: add it to any request.

items.text: Un tè e un'acqua, per favore.
items.means: A tea and a water, please.
wrong: Uno tè e un'acqua, per favore.
Un tè e un'acqua, favore per.

items.text: Ho un fratello e una sorella.
items.means: I have a brother and a sister.
wrong: Ho una fratello e un sorella.

Excuse me, how much is it?

wrong: Io parli un po' di italiano.

items.means: My mother goes to the city.

I miei genitori sono partiti ieri.

items.means: I'd like a glass of cold water.
literal: I would like a glass of

Ieri sera ho mangiare una pizza.

I want to see you soon.
What are you doing this weekend?

Stasera vado al cinema con i amici.

concept.line: The verb's ending changes with who does it: parlo (I speak), parli (you speak), parla (he or she speaks), parliamo (we speak).

words.means: sto = to stay; to be (how someone is)

concept.line: A verb's ending already says who, so Italian usually leaves out io, tu and the other subject words: Parlo (I speak), Piove (rains).

words.means: sono = I am; sei = you are

concept.line: Articles and adjectives match a noun's gender (la casa nuova: the house new), and so does a past form after essere or after lo, la, li or le: Lei è partita (she is gone), L'ho vista (her I-have seen).

words.means: ho = I have; hai = you have

concept.line: A yes-or-no question keeps the order of a statement, with your voice going up, and a question word comes first, often with the verb right after it: Dove abita tuo fratello (where lives your brother).

words.means: parli = you speak; parlo = I speak
capisco = I understand; capisci = you understand

concept.line: non goes right before the verb, and before any little pronoun in front of it: Non lo so (not it I know).

words.means: abito = I live; abiti = you live; abita = lives
vado = I go; vai = you go; va = goes

concept.line: Italian normally puts an article before mio, tuo and the rest (la mia casa: the my house), but drops it before one family member on their own (mia madre), except with loro (la loro madre).

words.means: lavoro = I work; lavorare = to work
